passage:
At five, Sumit lay on the rug and groaned, "I'm bored. Can I watch cartoons?" His mother Leela had a basket of old spoons, cups and a bowl of water ready. "Try a kitchen for your toys," she said. Sumit sighed, then began pouring, stirring and inviting his teddy to tea. He did not mention the cartoons again until dinner.

At fifteen, on a Sunday evening, Sumit noticed that he had spent nearly the whole weekend on videos and games. He felt a flash of shame, then stopped and took out a notebook. "What happened?" On Saturday he had argued with his friend Tanuja, and by afternoon there had been nothing else to do. He wrote: "Fight, then bored, then screen." He did not call himself hopeless.

Instead he texted Tanuja to fix the quarrel and asked her to go cycling the following Saturday. On Monday morning he put his phone on the shelf during homework and started again from there.

qa.q: What was in Leela's basket when Sumit said he was bored?
qa.a: The basket held old spoons, cups and a bowl of water.

qa.q: How do the two moments show different ways of handling boredom in Sumit's life?
qa.a: At five boredom is answered by simple materials that let him invent a kitchen, and at fifteen he reviews a weekend binge, finds the triggers of the fight and boredom, plans a cycling outing and restarts on Monday without self-blame.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling on Sunday evening when he noticed the weekend had gone to screens?
qa.a: Sumit felt a flash of shame, but he steadied himself and looked for the cause instead of blaming himself.

qa.q: What did Sumit change so the next weekend would go differently?
qa.a: He mended the quarrel with Tanuja and planned a cycling trip, which gave the weekend something to do besides screens.

grounding: Boredom in a young child answered by simple materials, and the same person later reviewing a screen-heavy weekend, spotting the argument and boredom behind it, and restarting kindly.
